lead: Numerical aperture, cutoff wavelength and diameter decide how a fiber couples to sources, whether it is single-mode at the working wavelength, and how much a joint loses. All three are read from light leaving the fiber or from an image of its end face. Field tests then check the laid route without cutting it. Only a few syllabi teach this measurement detail.
prereq: You need numerical aperture and acceptance angle, single-mode condition and the V number, and the OTDR from attenuation and dispersion measurements.

sections.h3: Numerical aperture from the far field

blocks.text: Light leaves a fiber in a cone whose half-angle is the acceptance angle θ<sub>a</sub>, so NA = sin θ<sub>a</sub>. A scanning detector records far-field intensity against angle, and θ<sub>a</sub> is read where it has fallen to 5 % of the peak (not the 50 % level). The simpler trigonometric method throws the spot onto a screen at distance D and measures its diameter A at the same edge:

blocks.where: A is the far-field spot diameter on the screen and D is the distance from the fiber end to the screen, in the same unit; tan θ<sub>a</sub> = (A/2)/D.

blocks.text: The index profile gives NA = √(n<sub>1</sub>² − n<sub>2</sub>²) (core n<sub>1</sub>, cladding n<sub>2</sub>), which agrees only approximately: the far-field value depends on the launch, so it must fill the modes steadily, with cladding modes stripped and a few metres of fiber.

The cutoff wavelength λ<sub>c</sub> is the wavelength above which only the fundamental mode LP<sub>01</sub> is guided. Below it LP<sub>11</sub> is guided too, but weakly, so a bend strips it. In the bend-reference method a 2 m sample in one loose loop is scanned in wavelength, then scanned again with a small extra loop that strips LP<sub>11</sub>. Their ratio in dB is flat at long wavelengths and rises below cutoff; λ<sub>c</sub> is where it is 0.1 dB above the flat level.

Cutoff depends on length and bending, so the method must be stated. Installed cable cuts off at a shorter wavelength than the 2 m fiber (the cable cutoff λ<sub>cc</sub>); standard single-mode fiber has λ<sub>cc</sub> ≤ 1260 nm, so it is single-mode at 1310 and 1550 nm.

The cladding diameter (125 µm for telecom fiber) and core concentricity are measured on a calibrated video microscope image of the end face, or, during drawing, by timing the shadow of a scanning laser beam. The core diameter comes from the near-field intensity or a refracted near-field index profile. A diameter error offsets the cores at every joint and shows up as joint loss.

sections.h3: Reflectance, return loss and field tests

blocks.text: Every joint reflects some light back toward the laser. Reflectance R = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>r</sub>/P<sub>i</sub>) (reflected over incident power) is negative, −50 dB or lower for a good connector. Optical return loss ORL = −10 log₁₀(P<sub>r</sub>/P<sub>i</sub>) is positive; the higher it is, the less the laser is disturbed.

items: Stable source and power meter. End-to-end loss at the working wavelength, compared with the link power budget.

OTDR. Locates every event at z = ct/(2n): a step at a splice or bend, a spike at a connector or break. A splice can read as a gain from one end because the fibers backscatter differently; the true loss is the average of both directions. A strong reflection blinds the detector for a short dead zone.
Visual fault locator. Red light (about 650 nm) glows through the jacket at a break or tight bend.
Dispersion and BER testers. Check high-speed routes; a bit-error test counts errors in known data.

spec.aria: A fiber on the left sends a cone of light to a screen 10.0 centimetres away. The spot on the screen is 4.6 centimetres across, measured at 5 percent of peak intensity. The half-angle of the cone is 12.95 degrees, and the formula at the top gives NA equals 0.224.

examples.question: In a trigonometric NA test, the far-field spot of a step-index multimode fiber falls on a screen 10.0 cm from the end face. The spot diameter at the 5 % intensity edge is 4.6 cm. The core index is 1.48. Find the NA, the acceptance angle, the cladding index and the relative index difference Δ.
steps: Acceptance angle θ<sub>a</sub> = sin⁻¹ 0.224 = 12.95°. Check: tan θ<sub>a</sub> = 2.3 ÷ 10.0 = 0.230, and tan⁻¹ 0.230 = 12.95°.
examples.answer: NA = 0.224, θ<sub>a</sub> = 12.95° (a full cone of 25.9°), n<sub>2</sub> = 1.463 and Δ ≈ 1.2 %.

examples.question: An OTDR on a single-mode route (group index 1.468) shows a splice whose echo returns 98.0 µs after the pulse leaves. Read from end A the splice shows a 0.12 dB loss; read from end B it shows a 0.04 dB gain. Find the splice's distance from end A and its true loss.
steps: Check: 0.04 dB is better than the 0.1 dB planning value, so the budget's splice line is safe.
examples.answer: The splice is about 10.0 km from end A, and its true loss is 0.04 dB.

traps: Using the 50 % (half-power) points of the far field for NA. The standard uses the 5 % level.
Putting the spot radius for A: A is the diameter.
Calling the operating wavelength the cutoff wavelength, or forgetting that cable cutoff is shorter than the 2 m fiber cutoff.
Reflectance and ORL signs: reflectance is negative (−50 dB), ORL is positive (50 dB).
Trusting a one-direction OTDR splice reading, or reading an event inside the dead zone after a connector.

quiz.q: State the far-field definition of numerical aperture.
quiz.a: NA = sin θ<sub>a</sub>, where θ<sub>a</sub> is the half-angle at which the far-field intensity has fallen to 5 % of its peak.

quiz.q: Why does the bend-reference ratio rise below the cutoff wavelength?
quiz.a: Below cutoff the loose fiber still carries LP<sub>11</sub>, which the small loop strips; above cutoff only LP<sub>01</sub> is guided in both.

quiz.q: A fiber has n<sub>1</sub> = 1.45 and a measured NA of 0.22. Find n<sub>2</sub>.
A connector reflects 1 µW when 1 mW falls on it. Find its reflectance and return loss.
quiz.a: P<sub>r</sub>/P<sub>i</sub> = 10⁻⁶ ÷ 10⁻³ = 10⁻³. Reflectance R = 10 log₁₀ 10⁻³ = −30 dB; return loss = 30 dB. That is a poor connector; a good one is −50 dB or better.

quiz.q: A far-field spot is 3.0 cm across on a screen 8.0 cm from the fiber. Find the NA.
A cutoff report gives 1210 nm but no length or bend condition. Why is it incomplete, and could the fiber still be used at 1310 nm?
quiz.a: Cutoff shifts with length and bends, so it cannot be compared with a specification. If it is a 2 m fiber cutoff, the cable cutoff is shorter still, so the fiber is single-mode at 1310 nm.

quiz.q: An end-to-end power-meter test shows 3 dB more loss than the budget predicted. Which instrument do you use next, and what do you look for?
quiz.a: An OTDR from each end, to find where the extra loss sits (a step at a bad splice or bend, a spike at a dirty connector); a visual fault locator then finds a tight bend near the ends.

beyond: Passive optical network installers test through splitters with OTDRs built for that job, and bend-insensitive fibers have made bend-loss tests routine. Search for PON OTDR testing and end-face inspection.
